activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Sophie planted little seeds in the dirt. Her grandma helped her pat the soil. "Now we wait," said Grandma. Sophie wanted the peas right away. But nothing happened that day.

Each morning Sophie came back. The sun came out. Rain came down. A small green sprout turned into a tall vine. It grew up a stick.

Then Sophie found something odd. A fat green thing hung on the vine. "What is it?" she asked. "That is a pod," said Grandma. Sophie pulled the pod off. She popped it open with her fingers. Inside were little green peas, all in a row! Sophie laughed and picked more pods. It was getting late, and a big pink pig statue stood by the garden gate. "Time to go home and eat our peas," said Grandma. Sophie held her pods tight all the way home.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Elias stood at the big kitchen table. Dad put onions in a bowl. "We will make soup," Dad said. Elias loved soup. He wanted to help make it.

Dad picked up a knife. The knife was sharp, so Dad did the cutting. Elias watched from his chair. He passed Dad the salt. He stirred the big spoon in the pot. Dad held the pot. It was hot, so Elias only watched that part.

Then Dad cut an onion. Tears ran down his face. Elias felt worried. "Dad, are you sad?" he asked. He whispered, "Like a little mouse, I will hug you."

Dad smiled through his tears. "It is just the onion," he said. "Cutting it makes my eyes sting and water." Elias looked at the onion. It looked small and quiet. It was not a mean onion. It just made eyes water.

The soup bubbled. Dad wiped his eyes with a towel. "All ready," he said. Elias carried the spoons to the table. Mom came in and sniffed the air. "Mmm," she said. Elias sat down and took a big bite. "I helped," he said. "And the onion made you cry."

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Sara sat at the kitchen table. Mama put a little cake in front of her. It was still warm from the oven. "Can you name your five senses?" Mama asked. Sara wanted to say them all. She held up one finger. "Eyes see," she said. She looked at the pink cake. Then she held up another finger. "Ears hear." She listened. The clock went tick, tick.

Two fingers more. "Tongue tastes," said Sara. "Hands touch." She patted the soft table. But now she stopped. One sense was missing. She thought and thought. Then she leaned close to the cake. She sniffed with her nose. Mmm, it smelled sweet like strawberries.

"Nose smells!" Sara laughed. She sniffed again. "The nose knows," said Mama. Outside, a bird sat high in the tree. Sara watched it shake its wings. Then she took a big bite of cake.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Isla ran to the big slide at the playground. Her friend Max ran to the small slide. "Big!" shouted Isla. "Small!" shouted Max. They laughed and ran again.

Max said, "Those words are opposites." Isla said, "Let's play the opposite game!" Max ran fast. Isla walked slow. Max was quiet. Isla was loud. Max sat in the sun. It was hot there. Isla sat in the shade. It was cold there. "Brrr," said Isla, and she put her towel on the cold bench so she could sit too.

Then Max said, "Sleepy!" Isla thought hard. She closed her eyes. Then she popped them open wide. "Awake!" she shouted. Max fell down laughing in the grass. "Your turn," said Isla. Max grinned and shouted, "Up!" Isla jumped up as high as she could go.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Samuel put on his coat for shape hunt time. "Find a square!" said Miss Maya. Samuel found a square block. He counted its corners. One, two, three, four.

Next Miss Maya said, "Find a triangle!" Samuel found a triangle cracker at snack time. He almost ate it. "Silly me," he said, and giggled.

Then Miss Maya said, "Find a rectangle. A rectangle has four sides and four square corners." Samuel looked and looked. He saw a circle clock. Not that. He saw a square rug. Not that. Then he heard the door open. It was Ben, coming in from outside. Samuel looked at the door. He counted the corners. One, two, three, four. Four sides too!

"The door is a rectangle!" Samuel shouted.

Miss Maya laughed. "You found a big one," she said. Samuel touched the door. It felt cool and smooth. The room went quiet as everyone looked. Then Ben knocked on the rectangle. Boom, boom. Samuel knocked too.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Olivia wanted the big red swing in the yard. Her cousin Sam wanted it too. They both ran to it. They both grabbed the chain at the same time.

"Me first," said Sam. "No, me first," said Olivia. Then Grandma came out. She looked at the cloudy sky and said, "We can fix this. Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another."

Olivia asked, "So who goes first?" Grandma said, "You can count to ten. Then it is Sam's go." Sam counted to ten. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Then it was Sam's go. Sam counted to ten. Then it was Olivia's go.

Olivia pumped her legs. The swing went up high. Sam held the gate wall and waited. Then they traded again. One go, then another go. The sun came out. Olivia laughed and said, "Your turn, Sam. I will hold the wall next."

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Logan put on his red shoe. "Baby store!" he shouted. "Follow me!" He ran to the car with Daddy.

At the store, Logan saw a tiny baby doll. It had a soft blanket and a cozy hat. Logan patted the doll hard, wham, wham. The doll's hat fell off!

Daddy picked up the hat. "A new baby must be touched very gently," he said. "Try again."

Logan slowed his hand. He touched the doll's hand softly, like a feather. The hat stayed on. The doll's eyes stayed shut.

"I did it!" said Logan. Just then, a real baby in a stroller grabbed Logan's finger. Logan smiled and stroked the little hand, slow and soft.

The baby held on tight.

"New baby," said Logan, "you can come home now."

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Mila sat at the art table. She had a big piece of paper. She drew a yellow sun. Then she drew a red apple. "What should I draw next?" she asked herself. "A dog," she said, and drew a small brown dog.

Next to her, Ben drew too. He drew a yellow sun and a red apple. The teacher called, "Time to clean up!" Both pictures went into one big pile. When Mila came back, she saw two papers side by side. Both had a sun and an apple. "Which one is mine?" she asked.

The teacher came over. "Look for your name," she said. Mila had not written her name. She looked down at her hands. There was red paint on one finger. Her apple had a smudge on it, from her own hand. She picked up that paper. Under the smudge, she saw her dog. "This one is mine!" she said.

Ben found his paper too. It had no smudge. Then Mila got a crayon. She wrote M-I-L-A at the top. "Now everyone will know I made this," she said. She smiled and sent her picture off to the drying rack.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Ellie ran onto the green field. Her team wore white shirts. Daddy sat on the bench by the fence. Ellie kicked the ball. Then she kicked it again, with her hand too. A big man in a striped shirt blew his whistle. Ellie stopped. She felt worried.

"That man blew the whistle at me," she said. Her coach knelt down. "He is the umpire," said Coach. "The umpire makes sure everyone follows the rules." Ellie watched the umpire point. The other team got the ball. A boy on her team stamped his foot. "He was mean!" the boy said. "No," said Coach. "The umpire is just doing his job."

Ellie kicked the ball again, this time only with her feet. The umpire smiled and gave her a thumbs up. Ellie ran fast. She kicked the ball into the net. Her whole team jumped up and down. "We can win!" Ellie shouted. After the game, Daddy opened the car door for her. "Good kicking," he said. Ellie waved to the umpire. The umpire waved back.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Brooks runs to the playground. The sun is warm. The swings squeak, squeak, squeak. His friend Mia is by the little playhouse. She hugs a toy bear.

"Let's play house," says Mia. "I am the mom." Brooks wants to be the mom too. He holds the bear's small hand. "No, I want to be the mom," he says. Mia makes a sad face. Brooks makes a sad face too.

Then Mia says, "When we play house, we each pick a role. You can be the dad, or the baby." Brooks thinks. He does not want to be the baby. "I will be the dad," he says. "The baby bear can be the baby." Mia smiles.

Broks rocks the bear near the toy bed. He pats its back, one pat, two pats, three pats. He sings a soft song. The baby bear goes to sleep. Mia claps. "You are a good dad," she says.

Brooks hugs the bear. "Next time," he says, "I can be the baby." Mia laughs and claps her hands. "Yes! And I will rock you to sleep."

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Clara went to the community centre with her dad. The bell at the door gave a little ring. Inside, a tall lady named May was waiting at a big table.

"Snack time," said May. She put down two plates. One plate had crackers. The other plate had apple slices.

"Which group has more?" May asked.

Clara pointed at the crackers. May smiled. "Let's count and see."

Clara touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the apple slices. "One, two, three, four."

The crackers had more. Clara clapped her hands.

Then a boy named Sam came to the table. He was hungry. May said, "Clara, can Sam have one cracker?"

Clara picked up one cracker. She gave it to Sam. Sam sat down next to a little toy car he had brought.

"Count again," said May softly.

Clara touched the crackers. "One, two, three, four."

Now the crackers and the apple slices were the same. Clara looked and looked. Taking one cracker away had made the number one smaller.

"Sam can have an apple slice too," Clara said. She pushed the plate toward him.

Sam took a big bite and smiled.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Lena sat in a big chair. The waiting room had fish in a tank. A little fish pushed a pebble with its nose. The peblem rolled and made a small puff of sand. Lena smiled at that.

Then a lady called her name. The dentist gave Lena a soft toothbrush. It had minty paste on it. Lena brushed her teeth, up and down. Her mouth got full of foamy bubbles. She was about to swallow them. Then she stopped. She turned to the sink. She spit the foam out. "Good job," said the dentist. "After brushing, you spit the toothpaste out instead of swallowing it."

Lena looked in the little mirror. Her teeth were shiny. "Can I push the button for water?" she asked. The dentist nodded. Lena pushed it. Water ran and washed the foam away. "All done," said Lena. "My teeth feel awake!"

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Raphael stood at the lake pool. The water looked so cool and blue. But he did not want to put his face in.

His teacher Miss Jo smiled. "Try blowing bubbles in the water," she said.

"Bubbles? Like soap bubbles?" Raphael asked.

"Yes, but you make them with your mouth," said Miss Jo.

Raphael leaned down. He took a little breath. He blew out through his mouth. Plop, plop, plop! Big bubbles popped up by his nose.

He laughed a big laugh. "I made bubbles! The water made them pop!"

"Now let's do it again," said Miss Jo. "Big ones this time."

Raphael put his face close. He blew and blew. Bubbles went everywhere.

Miss Jo clapped. Raphael splashed his feet. "Bubbles, bubbles, more bubbles!" he said.

Then he dipped his whole chin in. The cool water tickled him like a feather. He giggled under the bubbles.

Dad waved from the side. "Look at my bubble boy!" he called.

Raphael blew one more big bubble and shouted, "Watch me, Dad! Plop, plop, plop!"

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The TV went dark too. Matthew sat on the back step and frowned.

"No TV?" he asked.

"No power tonight," said Dad. He held a flashlight. "Want to see something?" He shined it on the floor. The light made a big white circle. Matthew put his hand in it. His hand glowed!

"What can we do now?" Mom asked. She found a board game. She found Matthew's book about the bus. She found his new puzzle with the ducks.

Matthew clapped. They sat on the grass in the backyard. Dad put the flashlight on a chair so it would stay bright. Mom rolled the dice. Matthew moved his little red piece. Beep, beep, he said, like a bus.

Later the lights came back on. Matthew looked at the TV. Then he looked at the game.

"More game?" he said. "And more ducks?"

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Aubrey wanted to make her own breakfast. "I can do it," she said. Dad made the toast, because the toaster was hot. Then he put the toast on Aubrey's plate.

Aubrey picked up the butter knife. She dug the hard butter with it. The butter was cold from the fridge. It made a big hole in her toast. "Oh no," said Aubrey. "My toast broke."

Dad got the butter dish from the counter. That butter had sat out all morning. It was soft. Aubrey touched it with the knife. The soft butter spread easy and smooth. No holes! "Look, Dad," she said. "Soft butter works."

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with one hand. She poured slow with the other hand. A little milk ran down her foot. She giggled. "Sticky foot," she said. Dad wiped it up with a towel. Then she tried again, even slower. Not one drop spilled.

The dog barked at the door. "He wants breakfast too," said Aubrey. She filled his bowl, slow and careful, all by herself. "Good boy," she said.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Zoey ran to the book corner at daycare. She wanted the bear book. The one with the sweet little bear on the cover. But the shelf was big and full.

"Where is my bear book?" she said.

Her friend Mia held up a book. "This one?"

"No," said Zoey. "That one has a dog."

Teacher Ben came over. He patted the shelf. "Look at the front of the book," he said. "The title is the book's name. This one is called Blue Dog."

Zoey looked. The big letters said Blue Dog. "That is the dog's name place," she said.

"You find it," said Teacher Ben. "Turn the book front side up."

Zoey held a book. She looked at the front. "Happy Bear!" she read.

"That's it!" said Mia. "The title is its name."

"One book, two books, three books," said Zoey. "Happy Bear is mine."

She sat down. She opened the cover. First page, then next page, all the way to the back.

"Read it to me?" she asked.

Teacher Ben sat on the little red rug. "One bear," he began, "two bees, three trees."

Zoey leaned on his arm and turned the page.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Eliana sat in the car. She was going to the dentist. It was her very first time. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "No," said Mama. "You get to sit in a big chair." Eliana wondered about the big chair. Was it soft like her bed?

At the dentist, Eliana was a little hungry. She had not eaten breakfast yet. She looked out the window. A truck went by. It made dust fly up. The dust looked like brown dirt in the air. Then the wind blew. The dirt flew away. One thing made another thing happen!

The dentist smiled. "Sit here," she said. Eliana climbed up into the big chair. The dentist tapped a switch. A bright light came on above the chair. Eliana squinted. The light was so big and bright! "Here," said the dentist. She gave Eliana little sunglasses to wear. Now her eyes felt better.

"Open wide," said the dentist. Eliana opened her mouth. She could not see anything. But the dentist could see! "Aha," said the dentist. "I can see all your teeth now." The bright light above the chair helped the dentist see inside Eliana's mouth. "You have clean teeth," the dentist said. Then she tapped the switch again. Click. The light went off. The room got dim. "All done," said the dentist. Eliana took off the sunglasses. "Can we go eat now?" she asked. "I am hungry!" Mama laughed. "Yes," she said. "Let's go."

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Edouard held his very first library card. It was blue and had his name on it. He was so happy.

At the library, Edouard saw a big dinosaur book. "A DINOSAUR BOOK!" he shouted. A girl at the next table looked up. She was reading. An old man was reading too. Edouard's mom bent down. "We use quiet voices here," she whispered. "So others can read."

Edouard looked around. Everyone was reading. He made his voice very small. "Can I have this one?" he whispered. The librarian smiled and stamped the book.

At home, Edouard sat on his bed in his bedroom. Mom read the dinosaur book to him. Then Edouard took his crayons and began to draw a big green dinosaur with sharp teeth.

"I will read it again tomorrow," he whispered, hugging the book.

Eliana stood at the gate. The playground looked very big. She wanted a turn on the swing, but the line was long.

A boy named Tom ran past her. "We go inside soon!" he said. "Miss Bloom will read the class rules."

"What are rules?" asked Eliana.

"You will see," said Tom.

Inside, Miss Bloom held up a big paper. "These are our class rules," she said. "We all follow them. Rule one is, we take turns."

Later, on the playground, the sky turned stormy and gray. Eliana ran to the slide. A big kid pushed in front of her.

The big kid looked at Eliana. "You first," he said.

Eliana slid down fast. "I like rules!" she called.

Eliana hopped to her spot in the line.

Mom smiled. "The dentist will count your teeth," she said. Brooks looked out the window. He made his plane jump from knee to knee. Soon the car stopped. They were at the dentist.

story:
Lillian wanted to see her happy face. She ran to the big mirror in the hall. First she smiled a big smile. The mirror girl smiled too. "I am happy!" said Lillian.

Then she tried a sad face. Her mouth went down. Her eyes looked watery. The mirror girl looked sad too. Lillian laughed. Faces can change like that!

Lillian made a scared face. Her eyes got wide. Then she made an angry face. Her eyebrows came down low. "Grr," she said. Mommy came to look. "Show me happy," said Mommy. Lillian smiled so big. Mommy smiled back.

story:
Parker put on his bear ears. He was a bear today. His friend Milo was a robot.

Parker wanted to tell everyone about the park. He started to talk. But Milo was already talking about his robot ship. Parker talked louder. Then Milo talked louder too. Now nobody could hear anything.

Their friend Nia held up a little bell. "One voice at a time," she said. She rang the bell once. Milo finished his story about the dark spaceship and the moon park. Parker watched him and waited. He held his words in his mouth like a balloon.

Then Milo gave Parker the red robot hand. "Your turn to be the robot." Parker took it. The robot hand went beep, beep, beep, all the way to the moon.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Sophia ran to the bowling lane. It was her birthday party! Mommy, Daddy, and all her friends were there. The shoes were red and shiny. The ball was very heavy. Sophia pushed it with both hands. Roll, roll, roll. The ball bumped the pins. Crash! They all fell down. "Again, again!" said Sophia.

Sophia held up three fingers. "I am three!" she said. Daddy smiled. "You were three yesterday," he said. "Today is your birthday. Today you turn four." Sophia looked at her fingers. Then Daddy carried in a real birthday cake. He lit the candles, and Sophia watched from her seat. She did not forget to make a wish. She blew and blew. Out went the candles! Everybody sang. Sophia ate her cake with a big spoon. "Best birthday ever," she said. "Happy birthday to me!"

Later they ran outside to the old slide. The grass by the slide was green, just like the paint. Parker laughed. "Blue and yellow make green," he said, and down he went.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
It was dress-up day at school. Levi put on a big red hat and a fuzzy vest. He wore it at lunch time. A piece of banana fell on the vest. Then he painted with a brush. A blue dot went on his sleeve. Then it was nap time. Levi took off the hat and the vest. He dropped them on the floor.

After nap, Levi wanted the red hat again. He looked and looked. It was under the coats! It was squashed and messy. His friend Mila laughed. "The floor ate your hat," she said.

Teacher Rosa gave a gentle smile. She held up a big basket. "Dirty clothes go in this basket," she said. "Then we can wash them." Levi lifted the vest up high. He threw it in. Swish! Mila clapped. "Two points!" she said. Levi threw the hat in too. It landed right on top of the vest.

The next day, the vest was clean. No banana. No blue dot. Levi gave the vest a big hug. "You smell like flowers," he said. He put it on and marched around the room. Then he found two paint dots on his sock. He pulled it off and threw it at the basket. It hit the rim and fell in. "Three points!" said Mila. Levi bowed.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jack ran to the sand pit at the park. A big pile of blocks sat in the middle. His friend Mia was already there.

Jack grabbed all the blocks. He put every block in his own pile. "My blocks," he said. He started to build a tall tower alone.

Mia sat down with an empty spot in front of her. She had nothing at all. Her mouth turned down at the corners. She looked at the ground.

Jack looked at his pile. Then he looked at Mia. He picked up a round block. "Here," he said. "You can have this one." He chose more blocks, one by one, and put them in front of her.

Mia smiled. "Now we both have some." She stacked a red block, then a blue one. Jack put a green block on his tower. Their towers grew tall side by side.

When they were done, they knocked them down and took turns stacking them up again. Jack clapped his hands. "Your turn, then my turn," he said.

The sun shone on the sand. "Same blocks, same fun," said Mia, and she handed Jack the last round block of all.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Beau sat on the little red chair. He had a big drum in front of him. He hit it hard with the stick. BOOM! The sound was very loud. A baby in the back row woke up and began to cry.

The music teacher, Miss Ana, came over. "Let's try something new," she said. Beau looked at the drum like it was a puzzle.

He hit it again, softer. Boom. The baby stopped crying. "That is a nice sound," said Miss Ana. "It is true," said Beau. "Little hit, little sound."

He hit the drum hard one more time. BOOM! The loud sound filled the whole room. Then he tapped it soft, boom, boom, boom. Miss Ana clapped. Beau smiled and tapped his drum all the way to the end of the song.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Declan sat in his car seat. The sun made the window hot. He touched it quick. "Ouch," he said. "That part is hot," said Grandma. Declan kept his hands on his lap. He looked out at the cars. Beep, beep, went a horn. The car stopped at the park.

Declan jumped out. He saw his friend Mia ride a bike. He wanted to ride too. He ran to her bike. He put his foot on the pedal. Then he stopped. He ran back to the car. "My helmet," he said. Grandma buckled it under his chin. The strap did not slip.

Declan pedaled the bike. He went fast, then slow. He fell once on the soft grass. His knee bumped, but the helmet kept his head safe. Grandma kissed his knee. "Try again," said Mia. Declan got on the bike. The fresh air rushed past his face. He pedaled all the way to the big tree.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Arlo had a red jersey. His team was called the Little Foxes. Every Saturday they played a game. Every Tuesday they had practice.

On Tuesday, Arlo sat on the grass. "I don't want to practice," he said. "I want to eat my juicy orange." Coach Mia smiled. "You can eat after practice," she said. "First we learn to catch."

Arlo stood in line. Coach Mia threw the ball. It bounced off his hands. Thump. It fell in the grass. "Hmm," said Arlo. "Why did it fall?"

Then practice began. Arlo tried again. He held out his hands. He squeezed them shut. He caught the ball! He jumped up and down. "I caught it! I caught it!"

Saturday came. The game began. The ball flew high in the sky. Arlo held out his hands. He squeezed them shut. He caught the ball!

"Wow," said Arlo. "Who taught me that?" He looked at Coach Mia. He thought about Tuesday. He thought about the grass. He thought about the ball bouncing off his hands.

"Practice," said Arlo. "Practice helped me catch!" Coach Mia gave him a big thumbs up. Then Arlo ate his juicy orange. "Sweet," said Arlo, "just like the game."

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Levi found a big cardboard box in the living room. He climbed in. "This is my car!" he said. "Beep, beep!"

His sister Mia ran over. "No, it is a boat," she said. "Row, row."

Levi frowned. "Car!"

"Boat!" said Mia.

Levi wanted the box to be a car. Mia wanted it to be a boat. They both pulled on one side. The box tipped over. Uh oh.

Mama came in. "How about turns?" she said.

Levi went first. He sat in the box. "Beep, beep!" said Levi. He drove to get a teddy bear. The bear sat in the back seat.

Then it was Mia's turn. "Row, row," she said. She paddled with a block. The bear rode in her boat too.

Next Levi had an idea. "Now it is a house," he said. They both fit inside. They fed the bear a crunchy pretend cracker. He was a sleepy bear. They sang him a song.

"I remember," said Levi. "The box can be anything!"

"Anything," said Mia. "Even a rocket?"

Levi grinned. "Count with me. One, two, three. Blast off!"

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Jack ran to the car. He held a small box. Inside was his new puppy! The puppy was white with brown ears. Jack named him Max. Max begged for a treat right away. "Okay, one treat," Jack said.

The next morning, Mom said, "Max needs a checkup." Jack frowned. "The doctor? Max can't sit in a big chair!" Mom smiled. "Not that kind of doctor."

They walked into a small office. Jack looked around. He saw a cat in a basket. He saw a rabbit with one white feather stuck to its cage. "Why are there pets here?" Jack asked. "Is this a pet store?"

"No," said a kind woman in a blue coat. She listened to Max's heart. "I am a vet. A vet is a doctor for animals." Jack's eyes went wide. A doctor just for pets!

Max barked once. The vet gave him a clean bill of health and a biscuit. Jack held Max's leash all the way home. "Max, you were so brave," Jack whispered. Max wagged his little tail.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Elijah sat on the bench by the ice rink. His skates were off. His toes were cold. Dad gave him a warm mug of cocoa to hold with both hands.

Near the bench was a big TV. A basketball game was on it. Elijah watched the players run up and down. They ran so fast. Then a man in stripes put a whistle in his mouth. Toot! The whistle was loud. Every player stopped running. They all stood still.

"Why did they stop?" Elijah asked. His friend Mia sat down next to him. "The referee blew the whistle," Mia said. "That means stop." Elijah watched some more. The players ran again. Then the whistle went toot again. All the players stopped again. Elijah clapped his hands. "The whistle makes them stop!" he said.

On the ice, a skater fell down. A fresh pile of snow sprayed up from her blades. Then a buzzer rang, and everyone on the ice skated to the side. "They stopped too," Elijah said. Mom blew a kiss to him from across the rink. Elijah pointed at the TV and smiled.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Isaac sat at the dinner table. His feet felt cold. He had kicked off his socks under the table. Mom set down his plate. It had ten little peas on it. "Count them," said Mom. "One, two, three," said Isaac. He pointed at each pea. "Four, five, six." He touched the last ones. "Seven, eight, nine, ten." "Good counting," said Mom. Isaac ate the peas, one by one.

Then he looked under the table. He saw one sock. He reached down and grabbed it. But his other foot was still cold. Where was the other sock? Isaac looked and looked. "I only have one," he said. Dad got down on the floor. He made a funny noise and peeked under his chair. "Here it is," said Dad. He held up the second sock. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks," said Dad. Isaac put on one sock. Then he put on the other sock. Now his feet were warm.

After dinner, Isaac helped Mom wash his hands at the sink. The water was warm and soapy. Dad washed the plates and cups. "Ten plates," Dad said with a laugh. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Isaac counted too. "Four, five, six." Dad helped with the rest. "Seven, eight, nine, ten." Then Dad turned off the light. It was still early, so Isaac picked a book. He sat on Mom's lap with his warm sock feet. "One story," said Isaac. "Two stories," said Mom with a smile.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Margot wanted to write a note for Grandpa. She sat on her bedroom floor with her red crayon. "Come read to me," she wrote. But her letters were all squished together. They looked like one long wiggly worm.

Grandpa came in and held the note. He turned it upside down. He held it far away. "Hmm," he said. "Is this about a stinky sock?" Margot laughed. "No, Grandpa! It is a note!" Grandpa smiled. "In English, we put a space between one word and the next. The spaces help my eyes stop and go."

So Margot slid her crayon along. One little space. Two little spaces. Three little spaces. She counted each one out loud. Now her note said, "Come read to me," with little gaps like hopping frogs.

Grandpa read it just right. "Come read to me!" he said. "Yes, yes, yes!" He got a book off the shelf. He opened the front cover first, not the back. Margot climbed into his lap. "Read the front page," she said. Grandpa turned page one, then page two. "You read my note," Margot said. "My words talked to you!" Grandpa hugged her. "Your words talked to me," he said, and turned the page.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Noah ran out to the backyard. His team was coming today. Dad had made a small goal with two cones. Noah put his toy horse on the grass by the fence. The horse could watch the game.

The other kids ran in. They all wore green shirts, just like Noah. One boy, Sam, wore a blue shirt. He was on the other team. Sam kicked the ball to Noah. Noah kicked it back. Sam laughed. "No, no," said Coach. "Sam, I am not late, I forgot my shirt," Sam said. His green shirt was at home.

Then Noah got the ball. He looked around fast. He guessed Sam was on his team, because Sam was close. He kicked the ball to Sam. Sam ran the other way and scored in his own goal. The kids laughed. Coach held up a green shirt. It was an extra one. "Put this on," Coach said. Sam pulled it over his blue shirt. Now he was all green, like Noah.

The game started again. Noah got the ball. This time he did not kick it to Sam. Sam had a green shirt now. Noah looked and looked. Green shirt, green shirt, there! He kicked the ball to Mia. Mia kicked it in the goal. "Hooray!" they shouted. Noah ran in a big circle. The toy horse sat still by the fence, watching the green shirts run.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Gabriel woke up and saw the sun. He was so excited. "Park day!" he shouted.

Then the sky turned dark. Rain hit the window. Tap, tap, tap. Gabriel could not go to the park now. His face felt sad. He sat on the floor.

"I wanted to swing," he said. A big tear ran down his cheek.

Mom knelt down beside him. "We need a new plan," she said. "Can you help me?"

Gabriel wiped his eye. "Okay," he said.

They got two chairs. Mom put a red blanket over the top. It made a tent. Gabriel crawled inside. "Wow!" he said. He brought his bear and his book. He shone his little flashlight. The tent glowed.

A loud boom of thunder came. Gabriel felt scared. He held his bear tight. Mom came in and held his hand too. The scared feeling got small.

Then Gabriel laughed. His fort was fun. He was happy inside it. "Mom, look! I am not sad now!" he said.

Mom smiled at him. "Come in, it's cozy," said Gabriel.
